In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In the first chord, the lower voice plays E3 and the upper voice plays G4. In the second chord, the lower voice plays G3 and the upper voice plays C5.

A. Oblique motion
B. Contrary motion
C. Parallel motion
D. Similar motion

In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In the first chord, the lower voice plays E3 and the upper voice plays G4. In the second chord, the lower voice plays G3 and the upper voice plays C5.

In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In the first chord, the lower voice plays E3 and the upper voice plays G4. In the second chord, the lower voice plays G3 and the upper voice plays C5.

The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In the first chord, the lower voice plays E3 and the upper voice plays G4. In the second chord, the lower voice plays G3 and the upper voice plays C5.

In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In the first chord, the lower voice plays E3 and the upper voice plays G4. In the second chord, the lower voice plays G3 and the upper voice plays C5.

In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In the first chord, the lower voice plays E3 and the upper voice plays G4. In the second chord, the lower voice plays G3 and the upper voice plays C5.

The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In the first chord, the lower voice plays E3 and the upper voice plays G4. In the second chord, the lower voice plays G3 and the upper voice plays C5.

The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In the first chord, the lower voice plays E3 and the upper voice plays G4. In the second chord, the lower voice plays G3 and the upper voice plays C5.

In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In the first chord, the lower voice plays E3 and the upper voice plays G4. In the second chord, the lower voice plays G3 and the upper voice plays C5.

In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In the first chord, the lower voice plays E3 and the upper voice plays G4. In the second chord, the lower voice plays G3 and the upper voice plays C5.

The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In the first chord, the lower voice plays E3 and the upper voice plays G4. In the second chord, the lower voice plays G3 and the upper voice plays C5.

In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In the first chord, the lower voice plays E3 and the upper voice plays G4. In the second chord, the lower voice plays G3 and the upper voice plays C5.

In music theory, contrapuntal motion classifies how two voices move relative to each other from one chord to the next. The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends. A two-voice composition uses standard scientific pitch notation, where pitches ascend through the musical alphabet (C, D, E, F, G, A, B) and the octave number increments at each C (e.g., B3 is followed by C4). In the first chord, the lower voice plays E3 and the upper voice plays G4. In the second chord, the lower voice plays G3 and the upper voice plays C5.

The four types of motion are defined as follows: 1) Parallel motion: Both voices move in the same direction (both ascend or both descend), and the numeric size of the interval between the voices remains the same (e.g., a 6th moving to another 6th). 2) Similar motion: Both voices move in the same direction, but the numeric size of the interval between the voices changes. 3) Contrary motion: The two voices move in opposite directions (one ascends while the other descends). 4) Oblique motion: One voice repeats the exact same pitch while the other voice ascends or descends.
